projects.title: JalTech – E-Commerce Advisory Platform
projects.shortDescription: Advisory module for a Colombian tech distributor that let customers self-serve and advisors act as order proxies — cutting billing time from hours to minutes.

problem.situation: Order-taking was 100% manual: a customer called an advisor, the advisor wrote the order down by hand, then it was keyed into billing later.
problem.businessContext: Colombia's e-commerce boom (2020–2021) was accelerating, but JalTech's advisors — spread across regions like Chocó — had no digital tools to keep up.
problem.userPain: Advisors spent over 60% of their time on admin instead of selling, and customers had no way to order without waiting for an advisor to be free.
problem.metric: Order-to-billing time → target: cut it dramatically

solution.approach: Built an advisory module: customers could self-serve their own orders, and advisors could act as a proxy — capturing customer data and mounting the order directly in the system, auto-billed.
keyFeatures: Self-service order creation for end customers
Advisor-as-proxy order entry with auto-billing
Automatic order confirmations
Order tracking dashboard

technicalDecisions.decision: Build the module on top of WordPress, integrated with JalTech's existing billing system
technicalDecisions.rationale: Fastest path to shipping without replacing infrastructure the client already depended on
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Tied future iterations to WordPress's plugin ecosystem, but avoided a costly re-platform

solution.mvpScope: Self-service ordering + advisor-as-proxy flow shipped first; checkout redesign, product descriptions, and mega menu came later as the platform evolved

myRole.title: Product Manager (first formal PM role)
responsibilities: Ran field discovery — visited JalTech regularly to map how advisors and customers actually worked, not how a spec assumed they worked
Introduced iterative delivery to a client used to large upfront releases — showing that shipping something useful in 3 weeks and improving it after beats waiting 6 months for 'perfect'
Prioritized MVP scope around advisor impact first, customer impact second
Trained advisors during rollout and ran a continuous feedback loop to prioritize fixes
keyDecisions: Shipped the advisor-as-proxy flow before full customer self-service, because it unblocked revenue fastest
Built a recurring listening loop with advisors (demos + feedback sessions) instead of a one-time handoff
Held the line on 2-week sprints even when the client pushed for a single big-bang release

results.headline: Billing time cut ~5x

metrics.metric1: Billing time: 2–3 hours → 15–30 minutes per order
metrics.metric2: Advisor adoption: feature was actively requested, not just tolerated
metrics.metric3: Engagement: single project → 18+ months of ongoing platform evolution work

results.businessOutcome: Codebulls went from a one-off vendor to JalTech's long-term platform partner, later redesigning checkout, product descriptions, and category navigation.

retrospective.whatWorked: Getting into the field with advisors surfaced constraints — like advisors working from tablets on the road — that never would have shown up in an office meeting.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Early expectation-setting on timelines was harder than expected with a client new to iterative delivery.
retrospective.nextTime: Would formalize the advisor feedback loop from week one instead of building it organically after launch.

projects.title: Raio – Spaced Repetition Language Learning App
projects.shortDescription: A science-backed, non-gamified alternative to Duolingo — mobile flashcards using spaced repetition, shipped on iOS and Android for a YouTube language-learning influencer.

problem.situation: The client had a clear vision for a spaced-repetition learning app but no spec, no wireframes, and no technical plan.
problem.businessContext: The client had built an engaged YouTube audience around learning English and wanted a product that matched their teaching style, not a gamified app.
problem.userPain: Language learners wanted an efficient way to actually retain what they studied, not streaks and badges.
problem.metric: Time-to-market → target: ship on both app stores within a year

solution.approach: Translated the client's vision into Miro wireframes — swipeable flashcards driven by a spaced-repetition algorithm — then handed off to Celerik's design team for high-fidelity design and build.
keyFeatures: Spaced-repetition scheduling engine
Swipe/tap flashcard interaction
Multi-language support
Published on the Apple App Store and Google Play

technicalDecisions.decision: Started with the Google Translate API instead of a premium translation service
technicalDecisions.rationale: Faster and cheaper to ship an MVP
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: The client pushed back mid-project on translation quality, forcing a scope renegotiation that cost 2–3 sprints

solution.mvpScope: Core flashcard engine + spaced repetition + both store submissions; deferred a premium translation provider and social features

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Ran discovery in Miro — turned the client's verbal vision into concrete wireframes and user flows
Negotiated scope creep, most notably a mid-project push to swap translation providers
Learned mobile fundamentals from scratch: iOS vs. Android differences, responsive constraints, App Store and Google Play submission mechanics
Used the app personally, on a daily learning routine, to validate the experience firsthand
keyDecisions: Held the MVP line on the translation-service scope-creep request rather than absorbing an unbudgeted 2–3 sprint detour
Personally tested the product to catch UX confusion before it reached users
Managed the handoff from the wireframes to Celerik's internal design team

results.headline: Live on iOS & Android

metrics.metric1: Shipped on both iOS and Android
metrics.metric2: MVP scope held despite repeated scope-creep pressure
metrics.metric3: Mobile release process completed successfully on both the App Store and Google Play

results.businessOutcome: Delivered a working MVP end-to-end, from discovery wireframes to store submission, for a client with high expectations and a fast timeline.

retrospective.whatWorked: Wireframing everything in Miro upfront gave the client and the team a shared visual language before any code was written.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Scope boundaries weren't documented explicitly enough upfront, which fed the mid-project renegotiation.
retrospective.nextTime: Would put a written scope agreement in front of the client before kickoff, not just verbal alignment on wireframes.

projects.title: Gold by Gold – Gold Traceability & Compliance Platform
projects.shortDescription: Centralized platform to legalize and trace gold from three sourcing channels in Colombia through export to Europe — replacing fully manual, audit-vulnerable paperwork.

problem.situation: Gold came in through three very different channels — subsistence mining, recycled jewelry, and industrial mining — each with its own documentation, and none of it centralized.
problem.businessContext: Exporting to Europe legally requires proving where every ounce of gold came from. Manual paperwork couldn't satisfy that bar or scale with volume.
problem.userPain: Five-plus internal teams — tesorería, radicación, cobros, exportaciones, operations — each ran a different undocumented workflow with no shared source of truth.
problem.metric: Regulatory risk → target: audit-ready traceability, near zero risk

solution.approach: Built a centralized platform to collect provider documentation, run gold through a structured legalization workflow, and generate audit-ready traceability reports.
keyFeatures: Centralized document collection per provider across all three sourcing channels
Gold legalization workflow (weigh-in → processing → export documentation)
Inventory dashboard tracking gold bars through each stage
Traceability reporting built for European auditors

technicalDecisions.decision: Pushed the providers/documentation module into production with the tesorería team before the full legalization module was finished
technicalDecisions.rationale: The founders needed to see the system working with real employees, not another promise
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Ran the legacy manual process and the new system in parallel during rollout, adding short-term overhead

solution.mvpScope: Providers and document-radication module shipped to production; the legalization module was still in development at handoff, with exports and advanced reporting deferred to a later phase

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Ran field discovery in Medellín across five-plus internal stakeholder workflows
Worked closely with two founders who had no prior software background and preferred concrete demonstrations over process explanations
Replaced formal spec meetings with twice-weekly, 20-minute live demos and short recorded explainer videos
Pushed for an early production release so founders could see their own employees using the system
Documented decisions and architecture thoroughly for a clean handoff to the next PM
keyDecisions: Chose tangible demos and videos over trying to explain agile methodology to non-technical founders
Released the MVP into production before it was fully complete, to build trust through momentum
Scoped advanced reporting into a later phase to protect the core delivery timeline
Handed the project off cleanly to another PM once scope grew toward a resellable product

results.launched: 2022 (providers/radication module in production; legalization module handed off in progress)
results.headline: Audit-ready traceability
results.businessOutcome: Founders saw enough traction to consider turning the internal platform into a resellable product. The project transitioned to another PM with full documentation of decisions, architecture, and stakeholder relationships.

retrospective.whatWorked: Tangible demos and an early production release built founder confidence faster than explaining iterative methodology on its own would have.
retrospective.whatDidnt: The five-plus stakeholder workflows could have been mapped even earlier to avoid mid-project surprises about how different teams actually worked.
retrospective.nextTime: Would build a full stakeholder workflow map in week one, before any wireframing started.

projects.title: NeverMissed – Missed Connections & Community Match App
projects.shortDescription: A social app designed to help people reconnect with strangers they encountered in fleeting, real-life moments — location-based matching, in-app chat, and a freemium model.

problem.situation: People frequently have brief, meaningful encounters with strangers — on the street, on public transit, in cafés — but have no way to reconnect afterward. Traditional dating apps don't cover this use case.
problem.businessContext: There was a largely untapped market for this kind of community connection, and existing competitors — dating apps, general social networks — didn't address the 'missed connection' problem directly.
problem.userPain: Users lost potential connections because they had no tool to describe and search for someone they'd briefly crossed paths with, and no safe, structured way to reach out.
problem.metric: Match success rate and engagement with connection requests

solution.approach: A location-based matching platform where users describe someone they encountered, and the app surfaces likely matches based on proximity, timing, and the description. A moderated chat layer lets both sides connect safely once there's a match.
keyFeatures: Matching search using user-provided descriptions, timing, and location to surface likely connections
Connection requests with in-app chat once both sides opt in
Location-based check-ins integrated with partner venue data
Profile creation with configurable privacy settings
A second-generation matching algorithm with more flexible criteria for higher engagement
Premium features covering unlimited chats, enhanced visibility, and location-based perks

technicalDecisions.decision: Added a flexible fallback layer to the matching logic for when strict criteria returned too few results
technicalDecisions.rationale: Initial strict matching returned too few candidates. A flexible fallback increased both match quality and user engagement.
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Added complexity to the matching logic, but the trade-off paid off in retention

solution.mvpScope: Core matching, profile creation, chat, and check-ins shipped first; social features and deeper geolocation integrations were deferred

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Led product discovery with the design team, including user personas and full user-journey mapping
Facilitated ideation and alignment between the founders and the UX team
Defined technical and functional requirements together with developers
Translated UX flows into actionable user stories and epics
Worked with the client to define system logic, data models, and matching rules
Owned agile rituals across the team, including sprint planning, backlog grooming, stakeholder demos, and retrospectives
Explored and prototyped monetization strategies
keyDecisions: Switched from strict to flexible matching based on early user-testing feedback
Prioritized safety and moderation features over shipping speed
Designed a freemium monetization model that gated chat volume behind a paid tier

results.headline: 3x more usable matches

metrics.matchAccuracy: Flexible matching returned 3x more usable results than strict matching
metrics.engagement: Users completed the match process and sent an initial message at healthy rates
metrics.adoption: Early user retention improved after the chat-monetization features shipped

results.businessOutcome: Delivered a fully functional MVP with matching, profile management, geolocation, and chat. The product continued to evolve with the client's internal team after handoff.

retrospective.whatWorked: Early UX testing caught matching-algorithm issues before full development, and safety features built user trust from day one.
retrospective.whatDidnt: The initial matching logic was too rigid — more algorithmic testing during discovery would have caught that sooner.
retrospective.nextTime: Would prototype matching-algorithm variants earlier and involve data science sooner to stress-test the proximity calculations.

projects.title: Colony Cooks – Ghost Kitchens & Corporate Catering Platform
projects.shortDescription: Multi-role platform enabling customers to order food from ghost kitchens, companies to organize catering with subsidies, and kitchen teams to manage orders and preparation in real time.

problem.situation: Colony Cooks runs ghost kitchens in Los Angeles, but had no unified platform for order routing, corporate meal management, or kitchen workflow — orders were tracked manually.
problem.businessContext: The ghost-kitchen market was growing but fragmented: companies needed an efficient way to manage subsidized team meals, and kitchen teams needed real-time visibility into what to prepare and when.
problem.userPain: Customers had no single ordering interface, companies had no way to configure subsidized team meals, and kitchen staff spent time manually organizing orders instead of preparing food.
problem.metric: Order accuracy and kitchen turnaround time → target: real-time, low-friction order tracking

solution.approach: Built three integrated platforms on one system: a B2C ordering experience for customers, a B2B corporate-catering flow with subsidy controls for companies, and a kitchen manager portal with real-time order tracking for kitchen staff.
keyFeatures: A B2C ordering platform where customers browse menus, customize orders, and have them auto-routed to the right kitchen
A B2B corporate catering flow where a company admin invites employees, sets partial or full meal subsidies, and configures delivery or pickup
A kitchen manager portal with real-time order tracking, filtering, printing, and status updates, including quantities, ingredients, and prep instructions
Stripe payment integration across all order types
A multi-role permission system separating customers, company admins, and kitchen staff

technicalDecisions.decision: Gave each role — customer, company admin, kitchen staff — its own backend logic rather than one shared model with role-based permissions
technicalDecisions.rationale: Kitchen-display tablets needed a different data model and permission set than the customer-facing apps
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More infrastructure to maintain, in exchange for real-time order updates and a kitchen workflow built around how kitchen staff actually worked

solution.mvpScope: All three platforms — B2C, B2B, and Kitchen Manager — shipped together with full Stripe and email integration; mobile apps and advanced analytics were deferred to a later phase

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Led end-to-end product delivery, coordinating frontend, backend, QA, and the client
Owned and maintained the full product backlog in Jira
Worked with the designer and developers to define features for each user role
Wrote user stories with detailed acceptance criteria and user-flow documentation
Facilitated sprint planning, QA cycles, UAT sessions, and go-live preparation
Collaborated closely with QA on regression checklists and feature-by-feature testing
Spent time observing kitchen operations directly before designing the kitchen manager portal
keyDecisions: Prioritized kitchen workflow efficiency over shipping monetization features early
Chose to observe real kitchen operations firsthand before designing the manager portal
Deferred mobile apps to make sure the desktop web version was solid for production use

results.headline: 3 platforms, one launch

metrics.mvpCompletion: All planned MVP scope delivered across the three platforms
metrics.qaValidation: Every feature passed full regression testing before launch
metrics.teamAccuracy: Kitchen teams tracked orders with zero discrepancies during UAT

results.businessOutcome: Shipped a fully functional MVP across three platforms. The client paused the product internally after launch, but all scope was completed and deployed, setting the foundation for a future catering-platform expansion.

retrospective.whatWorked: Observing real kitchen operations directly was crucial — those sessions caught workflow pain points that a spec alone wouldn't have surfaced, and the UAT process was thorough.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Underestimated the complexity of the cost-breakdown logic between customer and company subsidies — finance should have been involved earlier.
retrospective.nextTime: Would run Phase 2 planning (mobile apps, advanced analytics) in parallel to reduce time-to-impact, and prototype the cost logic before the full build.

projects.title: PrizePicks – Free-to-Play Game Mode & Seasonal Drops
projects.shortDescription: Free-to-play mode for a leading fantasy sports app, letting it legally expand into non-paid states with streaks and event-based minigames instead of real-money betting.

problem.situation: PrizePicks operated in paid U.S. states, but regulatory restrictions on monetary betting blocked expansion into non-paid states.
problem.businessContext: The company needed a free-to-play version that kept the core game's engagement without involving money, in order to reach new markets legally.
problem.userPain: Users in non-paid states had no way to engage with the core game experience at all.
problem.metric: User base expansion into non-paid states without legal risk

solution.approach: Built a free-to-play mode around daily picks, streaks, leaderboards, and event-based minigames tied to real-world sports and pop-culture moments.
keyFeatures: A daily pick game where users choose from a rotating set of cards and make an Over/Under prediction
Live scoring during the actual game
Streak tracking and leaderboard competition
Themed minigames ('Drops') tied to major sports and pop-culture events
Recurring bonus-streak events tied to specific days and themes

technicalDecisions.decision: Ran moderated live user interviews and A/B tests before locking UI decisions
technicalDecisions.rationale: A fully staffed UX research team meant decisions could be data-driven instead of opinion-driven
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Slower to ship individual UI changes, but higher confidence each change actually improved usability

solution.mvpScope: Daily pick game, streaks, leaderboard, and the first seasonal Drop shipped first; an expanded Drop calendar and deeper personalization were deferred

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Coordinated cross-functionally across marketing, research, design, internal developers, and DualBoot
Gathered requirements and kept the roadmap aligned across teams
Supported the design team with clear problem definitions and success metrics
Participated in live moderated user interviews and unassisted usability testing
Ran sprint planning, backlog triage, and delivery QA
keyDecisions: Prioritized entertainment mechanics — streaks, Drops — over betting-adjacent framing to stay compliant
Used real usage metrics (click-through, adoption, retention) instead of opinion to decide what to keep or cut
Adopted Linear for backlog and roadmap management for the team's speed and clarity

results.launched: 2024 (FTP mode); Drops program continued through May 2025
results.headline: New states, no real-money risk

metrics.metric2: FTP mode well received, laying the foundation for long-term engagement
metrics.metric3: Established a repeatable model for event-based 'Drops' minigames

results.businessOutcome: Enabled the company to expand its user base into new states without legal risk, backed by a fully data-driven UX research process.

retrospective.whatWorked: Live moderated interviews and A/B testing gave the team empathy-driven, data-backed confidence in each design decision.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Coordinating across five-plus teams — marketing, research, design, internal dev, DualBoot — sometimes slowed decision cycles.
retrospective.nextTime: Would set up a single shared source of truth for research findings earlier to speed up cross-team alignment.

projects.title: National Media – AI-Powered Media Automation
projects.shortDescription: Two AI-powered initiatives for a national media client — automating media planning and accelerating competitive advertising analysis — that cut manual work while keeping planners and analysts in the loop.

problem.situation: Media planners were manually extracting rate-card data, matching it against audience data, and building media buys by hand against strict business rules — a process that could take most of a day. Separately, competitive advertising analysis was also largely manual and slow to turn around.
problem.businessContext: National Media wanted to reduce manual work across two related but distinct workflows — media planning and competitive advertising analysis — without removing human expertise from either one.
problem.userPain: Manual matching and buy-building was slow and error-prone, with no systematic way to validate a proposed buy against business rules, and no fast way to analyze competitor advertising activity.
problem.metric: Manual process time → target: several times faster while keeping planners and analysts in the loop

solution.approach: Two AI-powered initiatives with the same client stakeholder group: MediaBuyer, which automates media planning by extracting rate-card data and generating buys validated against business rules, and Competitive Automation, which speeds up competitive advertising analysis. Both keep a human review step before AI output is finalized.
keyFeatures: Automated extraction and matching of rate-card and audience data
AI-generated media buys checked against business rules before being finalized
A human-in-the-loop review step for lower-confidence AI outputs
Automated competitive advertising analysis feeding into faster campaign creation
Status visibility for planners throughout each process

technicalDecisions.decision: Built MediaBuyer as two independent pipeline stages instead of one continuous flow
technicalDecisions.rationale: Lets either stage retry or restart on failure without losing the other stage's completed work
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More orchestration complexity up front, in exchange for more resilience against failures in the external systems each stage depends on

solution.mvpScope: MediaBuyer: rate-card upload through buy generation, human review, and export. Competitive Automation: automated competitive analysis feeding into campaign creation. Deferred: full history/reporting views and multi-market batching for MediaBuyer.

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Translated ambiguous business needs into clearer product questions and priorities across both initiatives
Connected National Media's domain experts with engineering and QA so business expectations and technical constraints were discussed in the same context
Defined confidence thresholds for AI outputs, routing lower-confidence results to manual review instead of treating AI output as simply done or not done
Translated media-buying terminology into concrete rules engineering could validate against
Supported alignment across both initiatives with the same client stakeholder group while keeping their goals distinct
Aligned a cross-functional team spanning backend, frontend, and QA
keyDecisions: Kept human review in the loop for lower-confidence AI matches rather than fully automating the decision
Scoped advanced reporting and batching out of the first release to protect the launch timeline
Prioritized reliability and audit trails over adding more automation features

results.headline: 5x+ and 3x faster

metrics.metric1: MediaBuyer: a process that previously took almost a full day reduced to a workflow reported as 5x+ faster
metrics.metric2: Competitive Automation: campaign creation speed improved by approximately 3x
metrics.metric3: Both initiatives launched with manual effort reduced while human expertise remained part of the workflow

results.businessOutcome: Both AI-powered initiatives launched successfully, meaningfully reducing manual work in media planning and competitive analysis while keeping planners and analysts in the loop.

retrospective.whatWorked: Designing for AI uncertainty from the start — confidence-based routing plus a mandatory human review step — avoided a 'trust the AI blindly' failure mode.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Some edge cases in matching and buy validation only surfaced once the AI was working against real data, not during early testing.
retrospective.nextTime: Would build out a larger test dataset earlier, before the AI pipelines were fully wired up.

projects.title: Awardees – Resource Management & Project Planning Platform
projects.shortDescription: Multi-tenant SaaS platform for organizations to plan projects, allocate people, and manage resource requests from a single system.

problem.situation: The client had no centralized way to plan projects, assign roles, track availability, or manage internal resource requests.
problem.businessContext: The long-term vision is a multi-tenant platform that scales beyond a single client to support broader internal team coordination.
problem.userPain: Teams couldn't see resource availability or allocation in real time, making planning and requests slow and error-prone.
problem.metric: Clean, testable MVP backlog covering core resource-planning functionality

solution.approach: Built four core modules — Projects, People, Requests, and User Management — on a role-based, multi-tenant-ready architecture.
keyFeatures: A people directory covering profiles, documents, roles, availability, skills, and allocation history
Project management covering project records, phases, and resource assignment by role
A requests module with a structured workflow for initiating and approving resource assignments
Availability and allocation planning with visibility into over- and under-allocation
A role-based permissions matrix separating Admins, Supervisors, and Read-only users

technicalDecisions.decision: Designed the data model and permissions system for multi-tenancy from day one, even though the first release serves a single client
technicalDecisions.rationale: Retrofitting multi-tenancy later would mean rebuilding data isolation and permission logic from scratch
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More upfront design work before the first client-facing feature shipped

solution.mvpScope: People, Projects, Requests, and User Management modules shipped first; a full multi-tenant onboarding flow for additional organizations was deferred

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Helped define the initial MVP scope based on business needs and technical feasibility
Structured and maintained the backlog in Azure DevOps, split into small, testable, role-specific tasks
Worked directly with the client and designers to shape UX flows and user journeys
Defined system logic, field behavior, and validation rules across key modules
Supported AI-integration planning for role recommendations based on user attributes and onboarding data
keyDecisions: Designed the People and Projects detail views around tabbed navigation for structured data
Chose to plan for multi-tenant scale from the MVP instead of retrofitting later
Aligned frontend/backend QA priorities each sprint to keep the backlog testable

results.launched: Ongoing (MVP modules delivered, platform in active development)
results.headline: 4 core modules shipped

metrics.metric1: Delivered a clean, testable MVP backlog covering core functionality
metrics.metric2: Four core modules shipped: People, Projects, Requests, User Management
metrics.metric3: AI-assisted role-matching logic scoped for onboarding

results.businessOutcome: Built stakeholder trust and alignment by documenting and validating each interaction flow, setting up the platform to scale into a true multi-tenant product.

retrospective.whatWorked: Designing permissions and data isolation for multi-tenancy from the start avoided costly rework later.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Still refining how much of the long-term multi-tenant vision to lock in early versus leave flexible.
retrospective.nextTime: Would map the full permissions matrix across all planned tenant types even earlier.
